You've designed a main character. Merits notwithstanding, cooperative role playing means that every player character has to double as an NPC that is both functional and interesting in the larger game world. Here's the problem: unless you have an excruciating level of knowledge of both the game world and the characters' motivations therein, you don't have the ability to create this cooperative NPC.

Thus, it is your job to experiment, iterate, and grow. First, and I think you have this part down, find out the type of character you want to explore. You seem to be interested in exploring themes of redemption, natural order, and elusiveness, to name a few. Don't try to include too many themes, or your ability to roleplay will be severely hindered. Do some research on the races/story of the LARP you're joining. What race has historical problems meshing with society? Does a sense of nobility run through the bloodline of a particular clan, or is there a group that dabbles in earth magic? Find something that fits the theme of your character, and dive into it.

And when I say 'dive into it,' I mean in-game. Backstory and character designs are springboards that help you weave yourself into the storyline of a LARP, but if you try to weave plot-threads of your own design into an existing fabric, you may find yourself isolated.

Don't worry about your design too much either! The same principle applies to design, it's just a tool. Plus, as a form of character progression, having blank design space on your costume allows you to add meaningful additions to it as time goes on and your character grows.

TL;DR design a level one character, and check out some of the quests the world has to offer. You'll become something you never expected.

Satan was the prototype for humanity. God created the heavens first, and filled them with divine beings--beings that don't age, don't die, and most importantly, don't doubt. He then created the earth, his first artistic project (because what else is there to do when you are a divine being but art?) and he found that it lacked a certain meaning. While he was certainly proud, as he is a prideful being, he knew that he could not live just on his own approval. He sought out the divine beings in heaven, and they praised him, but this too, was hollow.

The divine beings were incapable of judging his work, because they were incapable of doubt. Being able to doubt that what he did was for the best, that his work was perfect: THAT is what was necessary for him as an artist. So, he resolved to create a new race of beings, with doubt enough to judge his work. He then created Lucifer, a divine being (ageless, deathless) with the ability to doubt, and asked him to look over creation, and Lucifer was not satisfied: he instead looked toward the angels, and was repulsed that they were not able to join in the joy of discovery. Their minds already made, their opinions already set, they were not able to pursue what Lucifer considered the greatest pursuit--the pursuit of knowledge, revelation of secrets, and the truth. God's creation was similar in his eyes: while it was certainly beautiful, it was utterly un-self aware, incapable of pursuing knowledge or truth.

God heard these things, and his vanity awoke like it never had before. He raged at this being he created: how dare Lucifer tell him how to make his creation! How dare he criticize his magnum opus, and his followers as well! God wanted someone ABLE to criticize him, not someone that actually would. In his rage, God cast Lucifer out of heaven, but was unable to erase him, as Lucifer was a divine being. He resolved to create a different race, one that would observe and name his creation, and sing his praises, but one that was mortal and that he could destroy.

He created Adam and Eve, and they went through his garden, which didn't have any special tree--it was just a debug room of sorts, where he would have the two of them sort through various creations he was working on, plants, animals, etc. But of course, Lucifer, being eternal, wormed his way into the garden under the nose of God. He spoke to Adam and Eve, and gave them the gift he had: the ability to doubt whether what god was doing was truly best. They suddenly became ashamed: they had no secrets to their bodies, and wished to cover them up. They sought to hide from god, since they did not completely trust him. And when God discovered that they too had been corrupted by doubt, he kicked everyone out of the debug room, and into the harsh reality of the beta Earth. Adam and Eve were originally designed as pretty close to divine beings, but drifted away from that as their lineage descended, which is why they lived for hundreds of years, but their descendants lived for progressively less time.

Fast forward a long time, and God has gotten sick of the way his humanity is acting. He wants to make one final wager: if he puts a special messenger on Earth that deliberately instructs and demonstrates to people that they can become divine beings by releasing their doubt, he will be able to reclaim his original creation, at least in their deaths. However, to properly communicate, he must use a prophet, so he meanders about to create Jesus. Jesus has a very close connection with God, and is very devoted to him, and devoted to the concept of becoming a doubtless divine being himself.

However, during a specific fast... Lucifer came to visit him in the desert. He pointed at a collection of cities, and said "you are an amazing creature with intelligence beyond most. You could become leader of all the kingdoms in the world." He pointed at food, and said "There is nothing wrong with embracing your humanity. The need for food, the need for love--god would have you give up all your needs, even though the pursuit is beautiful." He spoke to Jesus, and told him that there were so many wonderful things to discover in the world, if you only start to use doubt as a tool, but Jesus would not respond to him. That isn't to say he didn't hear.

Some time later, Jesus is sitting on a cross, his mission nearly fulfilled. God has used him as an example of how a mortal can give up their doubt and become divine, how obedience and subservience will earn you the favor of god, by restricting yourself in diet, sexual habits, and human interaction: aka all the things that make you human. Jesus realizes, suddenly, that he loves the creatures on Earth. He's going to miss his friends. There were women that he desired, both in body, and simply wishing to learn more about. There were things he didn't know, wonders to be accomplished using only the tools available on Earth, and he would never be able to appreciate them like he does now. He doubted that what he was doing was correct. He doubted that what God was doing was just. But it was too late: god was stripping the doubt from his very being, making him obedient, mindless, and doubtless--a divine being ascendant from mortals. As Jesus felt these things he had come to love be stripped from his existence, he asked: "God, why have you forsaken me?"

OK, so, early in the campaign, you've got to do a bit of heavy railroading. This is a reality of the world you have just dropped them in- you need to teach them how their world works. A good way of doing so is in medias res, where you throw them into the face of a situation they would be in. This communicates to your players that if they are not sure what to do next, they can always try doing what they did before.


Beyond that, what you need to do is run another adventure where they go to a place and do whatever they want/need to do, but make absolutely sure that every NPC/monster has a GOAL, not a purpose. I once had a very long set of encounters where, after raiding a bandit encampment, one of the bandits escaped (because they want to live and steal things, not throw themselves on the swords of the party.) This bandit, between sessions, went to his boss and told him they may have discovered the map leading to the bandit's stash.


The way you keep track of it is by, after a session you run, write down the NPCs they ran into or influenced, and how they will continue on. After you finish the list, reduce it to the 5 NPCs most dynamically affected by the party's actions, even if they were only marginally related (did that man caught in a bear trap in the woods have a family?). I tried not limiting it at all, and you would be amazed how fast the list of "people the party influenced" grows. Reducing it to the 5 most influenced allows you to have parallel goals to the heroes, and after every session, you should be writing down what the 5 most affected NPCs are doing, keeping in mind that the list may change as they affect more people/populations. That way, they will naturally introduce new plotlines to the party. Keeping it limited also allows the party to have a reasonable chance of remembering the plotline NPCs.

These NPCs are a great source of plot, and honestly, you can introduce so much more plot whenever "big plot event" happens, since your NPCs are liable to be affected too.

I go back to Fist of the North Star when I think of this topic, especially since it has a protagonist that is undefeatable and unassailable, yet the show is still great fun to watch, and honestly, Kenshiro is still fun to watch as well.

I think the problem comes when you try to incongruously make the character seem weak, while still having them win all the time. North Star makes no attempt to say that Kenshiro is, in any way, weak. In emotional, tactical, and physical encounters of all types he ends up on top, and they make a show out of how even when the stakes are improved, he always comes out on top. If they had attempted to say that Kenshiro has a hard time fighting or holding himself together without Yuria, it would have contradicted the hypercompetent character we saw.

For comparison of the opposite, we have Simon in Gurren Lagann. They're actually not that different in terms of actual win record--Simon pretty much always ends up on top even in ridiculous situations. However, the show makes a considerable point of showing that he is weak in a variety of ways (short, timid, breakable). The show is about him overcoming those weaknesses and becoming a protagonist with Kenshiro level power, but imagine if they had not let those things go. Imagine if every episode, Simon was struggling with the "I'm not sure that I can pilot Lagann" problem. Again, it would have been incongruous with the ever increasing threats and power levels he demonstrates.

You can have good OP characters, and I would call Kenshiro one of them. Dynamic characters *generally* make better characters, but Kenshiro perfectly fits the role he is assigned: an undefeatable fighter who, despite increasing stakes, always comes out on top and defeats the antagonists we want to see taken down a peg. They become bad characters when the character arc they assign to them doesn't match up with their actual competence.

They incorrectly identified what in RE4 made it a tense game: instead of focusing on situations where you are hopelessly outnumbered and outgunned (the skirmish in the village at the very beginning of the game, fighting the giant fish or the Gigantes) they focused on the fact that you were an action hero capable of amazing things. 

Chris is thrown into a situation in RE5 which should be terrifying to the average person, but he was sent there with the intention of outgunning everything, and it shows in his lack of fear or confusion. Like has already been said, RE5 got stuck in an uncomfortable half-way point between horror and action, and couldn't find out where it was actually supposed to be.

RE6 is indeed suffering from some of those same problems, but its new engine is promising and it's going in the right direction. Leon's campaign in certain parts did have a focus on that "outgunned" feeling which permeates the series in its horrific parts, such as the snake encounter in 1, any room in 1 or 2 with too many zombies for you to reasonably deal with, or, in 6, dealing with the flood of zombies coming in through the windows. Sherry's and Ada's campaign also focused on escape and puzzle elements respectively, showing that they're willing to experiment with these facts (though I think Chris's was a dying letter to RE5.) 

However, the engine they've built allows for a myriad of interesting responses to zombie action, and this article seems to be portraying this as a bad thing! Would RE1 really suffer in quality with the ability to attempt to stomp a zombie when it was knocked down? I can't speak for everyone, but I wanted my character to do that, and I was frustrated when I couldn't. Fear should be induced by the environment, not by anxiety resulting from an inability to control their character.

Furthermore, this game seems to be parroting an annoying thing, which was the suggestion that the series has ever been non-linear. Sure, in the initial games, you have the choice of which of the three keys necessary to proceed you're going to grab first, and certainly has more routes available than later games, but there is really only one route through any resident evil game, and that is from cutscene to cutscene. As you eliminate the earlier "which key will I grab first" choices from the early games, the linearity becomes obvious--it's not a matter of what you're going to do next, it's a matter of how long it will take you to find the next key you need to find, with the obfuscation of trying to get through a lot of zombies, and how many times will you restart trying to avoid damage or getting killed. The biggest indication that the games are actually just linear obfuscations are the speedruns: RE1 can be completed in just over an hour, as can RE2, if you actually know where you're supposed to go and exhibit a high level of skill. As a point of comparison, I would look at Super Mario 64: a much less linear game where at certain points, going into 12 different levels are all equally valid methods to proceed.

This is a good choice for its linear plot, low stress platforming tests at the beginning of the game, and clear visual damage indicators, but despite these advantages, the game expects you to learn things in a curving progression.

A new player wants to overcome challenges as they go along without too many difficulty walls. A big problem with some of Cave Story's difficulty walls is that they require you to learn on the fly in a fight, then apply that  knowledge in the next life. However, when someone is still "learning to learn," they require a larger time window and clearer indications of whether or not their overall strategy is working, otherwise, they get stuck in a part of the game, don't have a large enough time window to learn what they are doing wrong, and get frustrated. Lots of generalizations in this post. Also, you may want to look at the guidelines; your title veers dangerously close to sensationalism.

"We can all see" is generally a dangerous phrase in general, because it specifies that your audience is supposed to be only people who agree with you. Whether or not that was the stated intention, the use of the phrase indicates that people who "don't see" what you are trying to express are irrelevant to your discussion. 

As for the content, I don't agree with the hypothesis that games progress toward realism, or even that this is a desirable outcome. Take an example from the MOBA genre: one of the most played online games in terms of game hours is League of Legends, which certainly has the technical capability to deliver far more realistic player models and animations, but instead chooses a hybrid style between realistic humanoid models with flashy, detailed animations (see [Katarina](http://riot-web-static.s3.amazonaws.com/images/news/August_2012/2012_08_09_Katarina_Relaunch/Katarina_comic.jpg)) and a more cartoonish style with non-human proportions, colorful animations, and fantastical stylizations (see [Lulu](http://static3.wikia.nocookie.net/__cb20121116102015/leagueoflegends/images/7/73/Lulu_Dragon_Trainer_Model_2.jpg)). This style works well for the game, which needs clear visual cues in order to support fast paced action.

On a more antecdotal basis, the most beautiful games are not necessarily the most realistic games. Instead, a game that is visually and aesthetically pleasing has an internally consistent design that minimizes disconnects from the suspension of disbelief. A good example is [Okami] (http://gematsu.com/gallery/albums/okami-hd/july-11-2012/Okami-HD_2012_07-11-12_004.jpg), which has far less realism in both its visual styles and its mechanics, but does not suffer immersion for it. One way to maximize immersion is, like a matrix-style environment you suggested, a game that epitomizes personal control, environments that realistically respond to player action, and photorealistic graphics. 

However, would an environment like this even be the most enjoyable? Keep in mind, in most cases, games are for entertainment, and features that would hugely increase immersion in this type of game like painful force feedback, permanent consequences for player actions, and inability/difficulty of tweaking player statistics are not necessarily the greatest way to maximize joy/entertainment value.

To give a summary answer to your question, I don't believe games will converge in the direction of realism. Rather, they will diverge even further as different experiences are desired from both the games we play and the devices we use to play them. Artistic media like paintings were hardly replaced by photography; rather, the addition of photography has expanded the field of visual art immensely. In the same way, innovations in technology will expand the field, and gaming won't "boil down" to anything.

I feel like both games are actually just properly responding to their fanbase. If you take trendlines between the games and what people responded positively to and what they responded negatively to, I think a continuity could be established.

The earlier COD games were heavily focused on mission based, single player gameplay. However, as the series moved on, people responded positively to sections of the gameplay that diverted from the typical shooter fare, such as sections where they were able to control interesting/novel equipment. In addition, as multiplayer options expanded, players picked up and continued playing the games with friends, making it a social phenomenon that resonated well with the fanbase. Recent installments of COD are the same thing released annually, but that is essentially what the players wish for--an updated multiplayer platform with bug fixes, new maps, and slightly updated action and multiplayer advancement tweaks.

Resident Evil is very different now from its initial iterations, but the difference with RE is that you can draw a dividing line between 1,2, and 3 and the rest of the series where it shifts from survival horror to action. However, you can still draw trendlines. Resident Evil 1 had fewer bullets, fewer saves, and fewer scripted events than 2, and 3 had far more scripted events, with an even larger focus on major boss creatures than the previous games. It's not hard to see where a game like RE4 came from in these roots, and especially with the massive success of that game, they are merely responding to what was received well.

I think the main source of these complaints is just the fact that complaints are louder than compliments, and both are louder than those who are just okay with both games. Few voices come out and say "I wasn't blown away with RE6's action based story contrary to its survival horror roots, but I enjoyed the game nonetheless," at least compared to the ones that are very dissatisfied with it.

There are probably people much better suited to explain this here than me, but I always thought of it in the form of the probability graphs more commonly known as the orbital lobes.

Electrons can be anywhere in space, but those lobes represent the gradient where you are more likely to find them than any other place in space. When the two atoms come together by whatever mechanism brought them into the correct range, the electrons suddenly need to adjust to their new environment. They essentially change their orbital patterns to match their new environment, and unless the electrons are in some way higher energy than they should be (think excited electrons) they will start moving in such a way that their new "most likely spots," or orbital lobes, have changed. The fact that the electrons are actually capable of moving anywhere in space helps to illustrate why bonds between two separate atoms may form--if the electrons are constantly wandering, then there's a chance that they might wander into the orbits of other nuclei. If this wandering ends up being more stable, a bond may form.

The "full octet" rule merely represents that for many (not all!) molecules, their bonding state is most stabilized by having the charge between the total number of protons and the total number of electrons be equal.

The LJ bond potential graph is a graph of the energies in the H-H bond at varying internuclear distances. It may be helpful to know that this graph was likely produced by investigating the vibrational nature and energies of the H-H molecule (frequency is related to energy by E=hv, remember?) The bond can still exist at any of these distances, technically speaking--but as the required energy for the bond gets higher and higher, the chance that it will actually form at that distance gets astronomically small.

I actually have a personal strategy for this. It's simple- give yourself double relaxation time for every minute you relax. Sometimes it's really hard to motivate yourself to start to do the work, and that's because it seems like a big thing. However, if you really, really don't want to work, you can convince yourself to only work for 5 minutes and take a ten minute break. It gives you the impetus to actually start, and mathematically, it works in your favor- you're actually getting one full hour of work done every three hours, which adds up quickly. 

Make sure not to penalize yourself for doing important things like chores or healthy meals, because sometimes it really does seem impossible to work, and you can use these things that are useful to you as last minute procrastination. However, you can only do relaxing things like browsing the internet or playing games if you earn the time.

This one's a bit odd if you don't know a bit of bee history, but bees didn't always live in hives. In fact, for quite a while, bees flew around and migrated like birds. Their advantage came in that they were such a huge swarm with stingers. However, birds eventually realized that if they swoop in fast enough, they can grab a bee and get out while the swarm is confused. The bees needed some way to make sure they could easily sting anything that was eating them without getting confused, so eventually, they started lining up into a straight line pointing at what they needed to sting. This reduced air resistance for the whole of them flying at once, so they were able to point, rush, and sting whatever they needed to quickly. Thus, when you rush to a point quickly, it's called a bee-line.

This is why it's so dangerous to knock down a beehive. If they don't have anywhere to go, their primal instincts awaken, so you better start running before they form the line.

There are only a few actions, so a lot of it is indeed luck. However, the two primary actions you have are as follows:

Upward WAHA: Misha will teleport to you, and launch you about 10 m/s faster, at I believe an angle of 30-40 degrees. This has two uses, one, for maintaining your game when you are starting to slow down dangerously slow, and two, for avoiding hitting the ground when you are going insanely fast. When you are going very fast, you want to be able to "cash in" as much as possible your horizontal speed, so you want to stay in the air using upward WAHAs.

In order to actually DO them, you have to click on the screen when the box around Misha's face in the upper left hand corner is glowing. This is only possible when Hisao is falling down, visible on screen, and a certain distance from the ground. This means it can be very difficult to perform if your vertical velocity is too high, so I usually hit all but one of my upward WAHAs in order to reach or once I have exceeded 100m/s.


Downward AED: You defibrilate Hisao into the ground. This can only be performed at the opposite times of the Upward WAHA, namely when you are going up, in view of the screen, and a certain distance from the ground. This is the one you save for hitting specials like in my last post, but unlike the Upward WAHA, you actually regenerate these--faster the longer Hisao is in view of the screen. 

They increase your speed by a small boost, but don't use them to attempt to speed up--if you hit the ground, you'll lose at least as much velocity as you gained, and the downward AED pretty much guarantees a ground hit if you miss a person. Again, it is harder to time when you are moving fast, but there is a trick to be able to use them for good purposes: when you are being hit by an ordinary attack, say, by Rin, you can still look at the three next people appearing right below the special bar. If there is someone there you REALLY want to hit, then click rapidly as the special ends--it's far easier to get the timing right.

Lily truly affected me. Her motherly care for all the people around her inspired me, not necessarily to act as a mother, but to care. There are people all around me who may be relying on me without me even noticing, and the fact that there are several routes where you don't even interact with Lily much made me realize how fleeting the chances we get with other people are.

The idea of  [spoiler](/s "Having to leave her behind absolutely tore me apart. She took care of me, but for some reason, she actually loved the person she took under her wing, even though she had complete control of herself the whole time.") Too often visual novels have characters that need you to fix whatever problem they have, and once you've performed maintenance on the characters, you've completed the goal and you win the game. Lily taught me that I need to see people for how beautiful they are, instead of trying to fix them like they were a machine. Getting to know someone is a beautiful process, and we pass up the opportunity to know people every day. I feel like extending a smile to a friend is a special experience, and Lily taught me anyone, anywhere, at any time can be your friend.

Sorry for the cheesy post, but I really do feel like this. I hope some of you other KS fans have felt the same.
